L57@P2-3: 2Abstract:
L58@P3: Recent interest in the ability of Desulfovibrio vulgaris Hildenborough to reduce, and
L59@P3: therefore contain, toxic and radioactive metal waste, has made all factors that affect its
L60@P3: physiology of great interest. Increased salinity constitutes an important and frequent
L61@P3: fluctuation faced by D. vulgaris in its natural habitat. In liquid culture, exposure to excess
L62@P3: salt resulted in a striking cell elongation in D. vulgaris. Using data from transcriptomics,
L63@P3: proteomics, metabolite assays, phospholipid fatty acid profiling, and electron
L64@P3: microscopy, we undertook a systems approach to explore the effects of excess NaCl on
L65@P3: D. vulgaris. This study demonstrates that import of osmoprotectants such as glycine
L66@P3: betaine and ectoine constitute the primary mechanism used by D. vulgaris to counter
L67@P3: hyper-ionic stress. Several efflux systems were also highly up-regulated, as was the ATP
L68@P3: synthesis pathway. Increase in both RNA and DNA helicases suggested that salt stress
L69@P3: had affected the stability of nucleic acid base pairing. An overall increase in branched
L70@P3: fatty acids indicated changes in cell wall fluidity. An immediate response to salt stress
L71@P3: included up-regulation of chemotaxis genes though flagellar biosynthesis was down
L72@P3: regulated. Other down-regulated systems included lactate uptake permeases and ABC
L73@P3: transport systems. The extensive NaCl stress analysis was compared with microarray data
L74@P3: from KCl stress and unlike many other bacteria, D. vulgaris responded similarly to the
L75@P3: two stresses. Integration of data from multiple methods has allowed us to present a
L76@P3: conceptual model for salt stress response in D. vulgaris that can be compared to other
L77@P3: microorganisms.
L78@P3-4: 3Introduction
L79@P4: Originally isolated in 1946 from clay soils in Hildenborough, Kent (UK), Desulfovibrio
L80@P4: vulgaris Hildenborough belongs to the sulfate-reducing class of bacteria (SRB), found
L81@P4: ubiquitously in nature (22, 43). These anaerobes generate energy by reducing sulfate (40)
L82@P4: and play an important roles in global sulfur cycling and complete mineralization of
L83@P4: organic matter. D. vulgaris has been implicated in bio-corrosion of oil and gas pipelines
L84@P4: both on land and in the ocean (5, 22, 55). Members of this species have also been found
L85@P4: to reduce metals in sediments and soils with high concentrations of NaCl and a milieu of
L86@P4: toxic metals (6) and to cope with salt stresses that result from environmental
L87@P4: hydration/dehydration cycles. An understanding of the ability of D. vulgaris to survive
L88@P4: high NaCl and osmotic stress will be critical to discern the biogeochemistry at metal
L89@P4: contaminated sites for bioremediation/natural attenuation and to predict the potential for
L90@P4: bio-corrosion of pipelines and tanks in soils, sediments, and off-shore oil production (8,
L91@P4: 36, 60). Availability of an annotated genomic sequence for D. vulgaris makes it ideal for
L92@P4: the study of complex SRB physiology (24).
L93@P4: The bacterial response to hyper-ionic stress includes a range of mechanisms, such
L94@P4: as aquaporins for water intake and functions regulated by the stationary phase sigma
L95@P4: factor, RpoS (12, 51). A commonly encountered response is accumulation of neutral,
L96@P4: polar, small molecules such as glycine betaine (GB), proline, trehalose, or ectoine (19,
L97@P4: 28, 31). These compatible solutes serve as osmoprotectants and are synthesized and/or
L98@P4: imported into the cell. The genomic sequence of D. vulgaris provides insight into its
L99@P4: potential responses to increased salt in the environment. While genes for trehalose
L100@P4: synthesis (otsBA) exist in the closely related microbe Desulfovibrio G20, homologues are
L101@P4-5: 4not present in D. vulgaris. Furthermore, no genes for ectoine synthesis or transport are
L102@P5: identifiable. D. vulgaris does contain genes for proline biosynthesis and an ABC
L103@P5: transport system annotated for the uptake of GB/choline/proline.
L104@P5: Compared to hyper-ionic stress, responses specific to Na+
L105@P5:  stress are less
L106@P5: understood, since they are often observed in conjunction with osmotic or alkaline stress
L107@P5: (14). RpoS-regulated genes have also been found to be responsive to Na+
L108@P5:  stress (12, 18).
L109@P5: Also often implicated are Na+
L110@P5: /H+  antiporters, such as those encoded by nha genes in E.
L111@P5: coli (14, 54), orthologs of which are present in D. vulgaris.
L112@P5: A comprehensive understanding of various stress response mechanisms required
L113@P5: the use of multiple techniques, addressing changes in different types of biomolecules.
L114@P5: Integrated analysis combining microarray data and proteomics are increasingly being
L115@P5: explored for studies at a cellular level. Although mRNA and protein levels are linked,
L116@P5: additional regulation during and after translation require that expression at both stages be
L117@P5: monitored for a more complete view of the physiological landscape (3, 23, 38). Though
L118@P5: not addressed here, critical information of cellular proteomic response also lies in post
L119@P5: transalational modifications. In this study, changes in the transcript and protein levels are
L120@P5: presented. These data sets have been complemented by preliminary metabolite analysis.
L121@P5: In addition, phospholipid fatty acid (PLFA) composition and lipid content, which are
L122@P5: measures of changes in cell membrane properties, have also been studied.

L132: ## Abstract
L133: Summary: Ceil mass, the average number of nuclei/cell and the content of RNA and DNA were studied in (Salmonella typhimurium during balanced (steady state) growth in different media. These quantities could be described as exponential functions of the growth rates afforded by the various media at a given temperature. The size and chemical composition characteristic of a given medium were not influenced by the temperature of cultivation.
L134: Thus, under conditions of balanced growth, this organism exists in one of a large number of possible stable physiological states.
L135: The variations in mass/cell are due to changes in the number of nuclei/cell as well as in mass/nucleus. An increase in the number of ribonucleoprotein particles at higher growth rates could, it appears, largely account for the increase in mass/nucleus. Calculations indicate that the rate of protein synthesis per unit RNA is nearly the same at all growth rates.
